title: Dirichlet's approximation theorem as a corollary of Minkowski's convex body theorem
description: A geometry-of-numbers proof of Dirichlet's approximation theorem: for every real α and every integer N ≥ 1 there exist integers p, q with 0 < q ≤ N and |q·α − p| ≤ 1/N. The result is obtained as a direct corollary of the gallery's integer-lattice Minkowski theorem (minkowski_integer_lattice_proved): the centrally symmetric convex region R = {(x,y) : |x| ≤ N+½, |α·x − y| ≤ 1/N} is realized as the image of the axis-aligned box [−(N+½),N+½]×[−1/N,1/N] under the area-preserving shear (x,t) ↦ (x, α·x + t) of determinant 1, so its Lebesgue area is (2N+1)·(2/N) = 4 + 2/N > 4 = 2². Minkowski's strict theorem then yields a nonzero point of ℤ² inside R, whose coordinates give the approximation. Mathlib already proves Dirichlet's theorem (Real.exists_nat_abs_mul_sub_round_le) but only via the pigeonhole principle; the Minkowski/lattice route — together with the explicit area computation for the sheared box — is absent from Mathlib and is the original content here. A corollary derives the |α − p/q| ≤ 1/(q·N) ≤ 1/q² bound.

overview.historicalContext: Dirichlet proved in 1842, by a pigeonhole argument, that every real α admits infinitely many rational approximations p/q with |α − p/q| < 1/q². Minkowski's convex body theorem (1889) recast such statements geometrically: a lattice point inside a sufficiently large symmetric convex body yields the approximation directly. The two-dimensional region used here is the textbook illustration of how geometry of numbers subsumes the pigeonhole proof, and it is the simplest non-trivial application of Minkowski's theorem after the two-squares theorem.
overview.problemStatement:
Can Dirichlet's approximation theorem be stated and proved as a direct corollary of the integer-lattice specialization of Minkowski's convex body theorem?

**Answer:** yes. Applying the integer-lattice Minkowski theorem to the symmetric convex region {(x,y) : |x| ≤ N+½, |α·x − y| ≤ 1/N} (area 4 + 2/N > 4) produces a nonzero integer point (q,p) with 0 < q ≤ N and |q·α − p| ≤ 1/N, and hence |α − p/q| ≤ 1/(q·N) ≤ 1/q².
overview.text: For a real number α and an integer N ≥ 1 there are integers p, q with 0 < q ≤ N and |q·α − p| ≤ 1/N. The proof is geometry of numbers: the inequality region is a parallelogram of area 4 + 2/N > 4 obtained from a rectangle by an area-preserving shear, so Minkowski's theorem forces a nonzero lattice point inside it; its coordinates are the desired p and q (a sign flip arranges q > 0, and for N ≥ 2 the half-width 1/N < 1 rules out q = 0). Mathlib proves the same theorem by pigeonhole; the present derivation instead routes through the gallery's Minkowski development, making the lattice-point mechanism explicit.
overview.proofStrategy:
1. shear / shear_det: realize the shear S(x,t) = (x, α·x + t) as Matrix.toLin' of [[1,0],[α,1]] and compute det S = 1.
2. box / box_volume: the axis-aligned box [−(N+½),N+½]×[−1/N,1/N] in Fin 2 → ℝ has volume (2N+1)·(2/N) via volume_pi_pi and Real.volume_Icc.
3. region_volume_gt: region = S '' box, so by addHaar_image_linearMap its area is |det S|·(box area) = 4 + 2/N, strictly above 2² = 4.
4. Apply minkowski_integer_lattice_proved (the gallery's ℤⁿ Minkowski theorem) to region: a nonzero point x ∈ ℤ² lies inside.
5. stdLattice_coord_int extracts integers q = x₀, p = x₁; unfolding x ∈ S '' box gives |q| ≤ N+½ (so |q| ≤ N) and |α·q − p| ≤ 1/N. For N ≥ 2, q = 0 would force |p| ≤ 1/N < 1, i.e. x = 0, a contradiction; a sign flip makes q > 0. N = 1 is the trivial rounding bound.
6. dirichlet_sq_bound divides by q to obtain |α − p/q| ≤ 1/(q·N) ≤ 1/q².
keyInsights: **The shear converts a rectangle into the Diophantine region while preserving area.** The condition |α·x − y| ≤ 1/N is a sheared version of |t| ≤ 1/N; because the shear has determinant 1, the area is exactly that of the rectangle, (2N+1)·(2/N), so no Jacobian bookkeeping is needed beyond det = 1.

**Inflating the box by a half avoids the boundary case of Minkowski.** Using half-width N+½ instead of N makes the area 4 + 2/N strictly greater than 4, so the *strict* form of Minkowski (already in the gallery) applies directly — no compact/closed boundary version is required. Integrality of q then collapses |q| ≤ N+½ back to |q| ≤ N.

**Geometry of numbers subsumes pigeonhole.** Mathlib derives Dirichlet from the pigeonhole principle; here the same theorem drops out of one application of Minkowski's convex body theorem, illustrating that the lattice-point count is the structural reason the approximation exists.

**Extracting integers is a lattice-membership fact.** The point Minkowski returns lives in the abstract ℤ-span of the standard basis; mem_span_iff_repr_mem turns that into integer coordinates, the only step connecting the measure-theoretic statement to elementary number theory.
prerequisites: Minkowski's convex body theorem for the integer lattice ℤⁿ
Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ, products of intervals, and linear change of variables (det)
The standard lattice ℤ² ⊂ ℝ² and integer coordinates of span members
